```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide

# Load in Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(sf)
library(tmap)


# Load in data
ej <- sf::st_read(here::here(
  "data",
  "ejscreen",
  "EJSCREEN_2023_BG_StatePct_with_AS_CNMI_GU_VI.gdb"
))

LA_crashes <- sf::st_read(here::here(
  "data",
  "SWITRS_LA",
  "Crashes.csv"
))

map_inequal <- sf::st_read(here::here(
  "data",
  "mapping-inequality",
  "mapping-inequality-los-angeles.json"
))


# Filter EjScreen data
California_ej <- ej |>
  dplyr::filter(ST_ABBREV == "CA")


# Filter dataset to a county
LA_county_ej <- California_ej |>
  dplyr::filter(CNTY_NAME == "Los Angeles County")
```


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide

# Check coordinate systems for compatibility
st_crs(LA_county_ej)
st_crs(LA_crashes)
st_crs(map_inequal)


# Quick test to see
st_crs(LA_county_ej) == st_crs(map_inequal)


# Change coorindate systems
map_inequal_transform <- st_transform(map_inequal, crs = st_crs(LA_county_ej))


# Check to see CRS's match
if (st_crs(map_inequal_transform) == st_crs(LA_county_ej)) {
  print("it's a match!")
} else {
  print("still not a match")
}
```


## Part 1. Legacy of redlining in current environmental (in)justice


### 1. Create a map of historical redlining neighborhoods
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7

# Map of Legacy Redlining in LA County

# Specifying dataframe from filtered data
tm_shape(LA_county_ej) +

  # Specify shape and customize specific attributes to enhance aesthetic
  tm_polygons(
    lwd = 0.15,
    col = "black"
  ) +

  # Specifying dataframe from filtered data and
  # set layer as main for map extent
  tm_shape(map_inequal_transform, is.main = TRUE) +

  # Specify shape and customize specific attributes to enhance aesthetic
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "grade",
    lwd = 0.2,
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Redline Grade"),
    fill.scale = tm_scale(values = "-plasma")
  ) +

  # Add a north arrow in the bottom right corner
  tm_compass(size = 2, text.size = 0.7, position = c("right", "bottom")) +

  # Adding a scalebar in the bottom right corner
  tm_scalebar(width = 8, text.size = 0.5, position = c("right", "bottom")) +

  # Add a title above the map, positioned to the left
  tm_title(
    "HOLC Redlining Grades in Los Angeles County",
    size = 1.0,
    position = tm_pos_out("center", "top", pos.h = "left", pos.v = "bottom")
  )
```


### 2. Create a table

```{r}
# Perform left join on the datasets
df_joined <- st_join(LA_county_ej, map_inequal_transform) |>
  st_drop_geometry()

# Count the block groups
block_percent <- df_joined |>
  count(grade) |>
  mutate(percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2)) |>
  select(-n)

block_percent
```


### 3. Create at least two visualizations summarizing current conditions


```{r}
# Color dictionary for colors that accurately represent the grade level
colors_HOLC <- c("A" = "green", "B" = "gold2", "C" = "orange2", "D" = "red1")
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7

# Find and graph the mean of LOWINCPCT

# Using the previously joined DataFrame
df_joined |>

  # Grouping by HOLC grade
  group_by(grade) |>

  # Calculating the variable of interest's mean and converting to %
  summarize(mean_pct = mean(LOWINCPCT, na.rm = TRUE) * 100) |>

  # Dropping NA values'
  drop_na(grade) |>

  # Piping in ggplot
  ggplot(aes(x = grade, y = mean_pct, fill = grade)) +

  # Specifying plot geometry
  geom_col(col = "black") +

  # Customizing color scale
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors_HOLC) +

  # Setting theme
  theme_bw() +

  # Customizing titles
  labs(
    title = "Percentage of Low Income Living in\nHome Owners’ Loan Corporation (HOLC) Areas",
    x = "Home Owners’ Loan Corporation Grade",
    y = "Average (%)",
    fill = "HOLC Grade",
    subtitle = "Figure 1"
  )
```



### 4. Write a brief paragraph reflecting on these results

Averaging the percent low income (LOWINCPCT), the PM2.5 percentile (P_PM25), and the low life expectancy percentile (P_LIFEEXPPCT) across census block groups in each HOLC grade shows a consistent pattern that conditions worsen steadily from Grade A to Grade D. In Figure 1, block groups in Grade D areas average nearly 40% low-income residents, compared with about 15% in Grade A areas. Figure 3 shows a similar gradient, with Grade D areas averaging around the 55th percentile for low life expectancy versus roughly the 25th percentile for Grade A. Figure 2 shows the same ordering for PM2.5, but the differences are much smaller. Every grade falls above the 70th percentile, which likely reflects poor air quality across Los Angeles county as a whole. Together, the results from these figures suggest that the effects of redlining persist nearly a century later. Neighborhoods rated worse than others were historically denied investment within the community, which made them targets for more highways and industrial land uses. It is important to consider that these averages show association rather than causation, and they do not explicitly show the variation within each grade.
